  ensures index == -1 <==>
    forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] != key

  ensures index != -1 ==>
    0 <= index < a.Length && a[index] == key

requires is the condition the caller must satisfy: the array is sorted in ascending order. Equal values are allowed.

The first ensures says the result is -1 if and only if the value is absent. The second says that any other result must be a valid index containing the value. If there are duplicates, returning any matching index is fine; this contract doesn't ask for the first one.

In other words, there are two cases: if the value is missing, return -1; if it exists, return an index where it appears. Both clauses work together: the first describes when -1 is allowed, and the second checks that any other result points to the value.

The implementation needs an explanation too

Here is the complete method, including the loop invariants:

method BinarySearch(a: array<int>, key: int) returns (index: int)
  requires forall i, j ::
    0 <= i < j < a.Length ==> a[i] <= a[j]
  ensures index == -1 <==>
    forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] != key
  ensures index != -1 ==>
    0 <= index < a.Length && a[index] == key
{
  var low := 0;
  var high := a.Length;

  while low < high
    invariant 0 <= low <= high <= a.Length
    invariant forall k :: 0 <= k < low ==> a[k] < key
    invariant forall k :: high <= k < a.Length ==> key < a[k]
    decreases high - low
  {
    var mid := low + (high - low) / 2;

    if a[mid] < key {
      low := mid + 1;
    } else if key < a[mid] {
      high := mid;
    } else {
      return mid;
    }
  }

  return -1;
}

The search range is [low, high): it includes low, but not high. At the beginning, that's the whole array. At the end, when low == high, there's nothing left to search.

The invariants describe what must remain true throughout the loop. The first keeps the range inside the array. The other two say that everything before low is smaller than the key, and everything at or after high is larger. If we find the key, we return its index. If the range becomes empty, those two facts explain why the key can't be anywhere in the array.

decreases high - low is the termination argument. The verifier checks that the remaining range gets smaller on each iteration that continues the loop. Without that check, we could miss a search that gets stuck repeating the same step.

With Dafny 4.11.0, the verifier reported:

Dafny program verifier finished with 3 verified, 0 errors

Those three verified items are the verifier's reported count for the sample; they aren't a count of all the individual properties. The method's contract, bounds and termination are checked under its precondition. Dafny's guide goes into more detail on preconditions, postconditions and invariants.

Getting Started with Dafny: A Guide | Dafny Documentation

dafny.org

Let's break it

I changed one line:

- low := mid + 1;
+ low := mid;

The middle value is too small, so moving the lower bound to the middle might seem reasonable. But we already checked that position; we need to move past it.

Suppose we're looking for 6 and only 5 remains. low and mid are both 2, so setting low to mid leaves the range exactly where it was:

The next iteration checks 5 again, and the one after that does the same. With low := mid + 1, low becomes 3, the range is empty, and the search returns -1.

Dafny rejected the changed version:

Error: decreases expression might not decrease

Dafny program verifier finished with 2 verified, 1 error

The error doesn't spell out the one-element case, but it points us to the right place: the search range isn't guaranteed to shrink.

But I write JavaScript

Dafny can compile to JavaScript. I compiled this sample with dafny build --target js and ran the generated program with Node. For [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], it returned 3 for 7 and -1 for 4.

Installation Instructions | Dafny Documentation

dafny.org

The generated JavaScript uses bignumber.js for Dafny integers. It also includes generated runtime code, so this isn't the same experience as adding a type annotation to an existing JavaScript function. To call the generated method from an application, we need an integration layer that supplies values in the expected representation. I tried that separately with a small session-policy function; the generated sample needed an export added before a Node wrapper could call it.

And remember the first rule? The array must be sorted. Dafny checks that calls from verified Dafny code satisfy the requires clause; our sample's Main does. But the search method itself assumes its input is sorted, and the generated JavaScript doesn't automatically check an array supplied by a JavaScript caller. We need to establish that guarantee at the boundary or elsewhere in the application. Checking every element on every call takes linear time, which can outweigh the benefit of binary search.

We also need to check how the JavaScript adapter converts values. Dafny integers are mathematical integers; JavaScript Number values have their own limits.

The proof also doesn't establish that we picked the right behavior. If the product needs the first occurrence of a duplicate, our current contract allows a different matching index. Dafny can verify exactly what we asked for and still leave the product team asking why the result isn't the one they expected.

How is this different from TDD?

With TDD, I could start with a failing test for searching [5] for 6, then write the search until that test passes. That case would expose the broken low := mid update, although the test runner would need a timeout because the function gets stuck. I'd also add tests for an empty array, a value at either end, a missing value and duplicates.

Those tests check the inputs I chose. Dafny checks the method against the contract for all sorted integer arrays in its model, including the cases I didn't think to write down. It also checks that the loop makes progress, so I don't have to wait for a particular test to hang before finding that problem.

There's a tradeoff: I had to write the contract and loop invariants. If I forget to specify that the result should be the first matching index, Dafny won't invent that requirement for me. A test can miss the same requirement, but it's often easier to write and read a concrete example of what a user expects.

I'd still use tests around the generated JavaScript: they can check the adapter and real inputs from the application, which sit outside this proof. TDD would help me develop those behaviors one example at a time; Dafny gives me a way to check a general rule about the search itself.

What changes with AI?

Formal verification isn't new. What's changing for me is how practical it feels to try it. Learning a verification language, writing the specification and working out the loop invariants all take time. On top of building the feature, that can make verification a difficult sell.

Here, a coding agent helped write the Dafny example and work through the verification. That gave me something concrete to read and experiment with instead of starting from a blank file. I could change mid + 1 to mid, run the verifier again and see what happened. Getting to that point took less effort than learning the whole tool before trying a small example.

That doesn't mean I can accept whatever the agent writes. I still need to understand the contract well enough to notice that it allows any matching index, and check what happens when the code is called from JavaScript. But if AI can help with the mechanics and make these experiments cheaper, formal verification becomes something more of us can try on code where it would previously have been hard to justify the time.

articles.title: AI found the vulnerability. Are we done yet?
articles.description: AI is finding serious vulnerabilities and writing increasingly capable code. PHP2Shell and Firefox show why proving, fixing and shipping those findings is still hard work.
articles.body_html:
What caught my attention about PHP2Shell was the PHP team's explanation of why fixing it took so long. A developer had noticed signs of the problem back in 2024. They had several possible fixes, but each came with problems: breaking compatibility, creating denial-of-service risks, or requiring changes to third-party extensions.

Imagine knowing there's a security problem in your code and having to choose which other problem you're willing to create to fix it. Now imagine that code is PHP.

AI helped researchers turn these flaws into working exploits. That's a big deal. But reading the maintainers' account, I kept coming back to everything they had to work through before they could ship a fix.

In October, PHP released emergency security updates for two critical vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell. They affect the PHP engine itself, and under the right conditions can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on a vulnerable server.

Finding a flaw, demonstrating an exploit, fixing the underlying problem and safely deploying that fix are different jobs. Being good at one doesn't automatically finish the others.

And before anyone puts off updating PHP because an exploit sounds difficult: please don't. Security researchers have demonstrated working attacks, and NVISO's October 28 update cited reports of targeted exploitation. Difficulty is not a security patch.

Ok, but the AI found it. Isn't that the hard part?

It's a hard part. And in this case the models helped with more than just finding the bugs.

According to Wiz, the flaws involve how PHP handles fatal errors, especially out-of-memory failures. An interrupted request can leave internal state partially initialized or pointing at freed memory. Later processing may reuse that invalid state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.

The first signs of the out-of-memory problem appeared while a PHP developer was fixing an issue from a 2024 security audit. A possible exploit was theorized, but no concrete path to remote code execution had been established at the time.

The Foundation describes the stalled decision on a fix as a structural failure involving both the team's process and limited resources. Reports from Calif, OpenAI and Wiz in 2026 made the impact clearer, and the security team prioritized a fix across supported PHP versions.

Wiz says frontier models helped it develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. Each target still required testing, debugging and adaptation to its memory layout.

Finding the crack is a start. The rest of the mechanism still matters.

The distinction mattered after disclosure too. In its October 28 guidance, NVISO cited a report of targeted compromise and a successful attack against a challenge server, with a public proof of concept. It had not observed successful exploitation in its own telemetry. There was no reliable universal public exploit at that point, and many non-functional tools were being circulated.

AWS identified attempted exploits against its honeypot before public disclosure, but couldn't tell whether they would have succeeded against real systems. When a model generates an exploit, I'd ask the same question: what shows that it actually works? Sending a payload or getting a convincing explanation isn't enough. We need to reproduce the result under realistic conditions.

What happened with Firefox?

Mozilla used a security analysis pipeline with Claude Mythos Preview and other models to investigate Firefox. Its engineers reported that Firefox 150 included fixes for 271 vulnerabilities identified with Mythos Preview. Their technical write-up describes findings across different browser components, including some involving sandbox escapes and bugs that had been around for years.

Some of those sandbox escape reports assume an attacker has already compromised a content process. Escaping the sandbox is a serious vulnerability, but a complete browser attack would also need a way to compromise that process first.

That's a lot of real bugs. Mozilla also says the improvement came from both more capable models and the work it put into the pipeline: steering the models, filtering reports and giving them a way to produce test cases. The pipeline was adapted to Firefox, with feedback from the engineers handling the reports.

Mozilla says more than 100 people contributed code to the effort, with others involved in triage, testing and releases. In an interview with TechCrunch, Mozilla's Brian Grinstead said that, for the bugs discussed there, an engineer wrote each patch and another reviewed it. The team also asked AI for suggested patches, but those generally weren't ready to deploy directly.

A finding still has to become a fix people can safely use.

What does a working fix actually prove?

With PHP, stopping one proof of concept wasn't enough. The fix had to address memory management and error handling across supported versions.

If the agent's patch stops the exploit, I still want to know: does it address the underlying failure across the affected paths? Does it introduce a different way to exhaust memory? Does it work on the supported versions without breaking extensions? Passing the test for one exploit isn't proof that we've fixed the whole problem.

What do the benchmarks tell us?

SecureVibeBench reconstructs 105 C/C++ implementation tasks from changes that introduced real vulnerabilities. The agents implement the original requirements, rather than patch an already identified bug. In the June 2026 version of the paper, the best tested combination, SWE-agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5, met both the functionality and security criteria on 23.8% of those tasks.

These were specific, difficult tasks using models from 2025, not the newer frontier systems in the PHP and Firefox examples above. The result doesn't tell us how those newer models would perform. What I find useful is the question the benchmark asks: did the change meet the functional requirement without introducing a security problem?

For PHP, a benchmark score won't tell us whether a proposed patch handles each affected configuration. For Firefox, it won't tell us whether a sandbox escape starts from an already compromised process. Those answers have to come from investigating the actual behavior and checking the evidence.

So what do we do with the findings?

I'd use AI to find the bug and help fix it. But if I can't explain why the patch works, I'm not ready to ship it.

articles.title: I Re-Encoded the Same Eight Bytes Four Million Times
articles.description: A server-sent-events writer was allocating a fresh byte[] for its constant framing on every record. Switching to C#'s u8 literals cut 122 MB of garbage per pass and ran about 3x faster.
articles.body_html:
I was writing a small server-sent-events endpoint — nothing clever, just streaming records to a browser as they came off a queue. Each record goes out framed: data: in front, a blank line behind. I wrote the obvious thing, it worked, and I forgot about it. Then I was poking at an allocation profile for something unrelated and saw a wall of tiny byte[] allocations coming out of that writer. The payloads I understood. The framing I did not. Those two little strings never changed, so why was the loop minting fresh arrays for them a few million times a second?

Here's the loop that did it:

for (int i = 0; i < Records; i++)
{
    buffer.Write(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("data: "));
    buffer.Write(payload);
    buffer.Write(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("\n\n"));
}

Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("data: ") does exactly what it says every single time: it allocates a brand-new six-byte array, fills it, hands it to Write, and then it's garbage. Same for the "\n\n". The string is a compile-time constant, the bytes can never differ between iterations, and I was still paying for a fresh array on every pass. Two constant tokens, two allocations per record, nothing to show for it afterward.

The literal that isn't a string

C# has a thing for this now, and it's been stable for a few language versions: the u8 suffix. Write "data: "u8 and you don't get a string, you get a ReadOnlySpan<byte> that points straight at a blob the compiler bakes into the assembly's data section. No encoding step at runtime. No array. Reading it is just handing out a view over bytes that were already there when the program loaded.

The one wrinkle is that a ReadOnlySpan<byte> is a ref struct, so you can't drop it in a field and keep it around. The idiom that gets you a name for it is a property:

static class Framing
{
    public static ReadOnlySpan<byte> Prefix => "data: "u8;
    public static ReadOnlySpan<byte> Suffix => "\n\n"u8;
}

Every read of Framing.Prefix returns a span over the same static bytes. Nothing is copied, nothing is allocated. The loop turns into this:

for (int i = 0; i < Records; i++)
{
    buffer.Write(Framing.Prefix);
    buffer.Write(payload);
    buffer.Write(Framing.Suffix);
}

Stream.Write already takes a ReadOnlySpan<byte>, so the span goes in with no detour through an array at all.

What it actually bought me

I measured it the way I measure most of this stuff: GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around the work, best-of-five on a Stopwatch for the timing. I framed two million records each pass. The allocation number is the one I trust, because it's deterministic and doesn't wobble between runs the way milliseconds do.

GetBytes per write    best  109 ms    183.1 MB/pass   gen0=7   (checksum 54000000)
u8 literal            best   38 ms     61.0 MB/pass    gen0=2   (checksum 54000000)

The checksums match — same 54 million bytes come out either way, so this isn't a correctness trade. The framing arrays were 122 MB of garbage per pass, gone. Gen0 collections dropped from seven to two. And it ran about three times faster, though I'd lean on the allocation figure over the timing since the clock jumps around on a shared box.

Now the honest part, because 61 MB is not zero and I don't want to pretend it is. That leftover is the output buffer itself. I sized the MemoryStream to hold the whole batch, so there's one big array per pass by design, and that one's the real work. The u8 change didn't make the method allocation-free, it deleted the allocations that had no business existing: the four million throwaway arrays for eight constant bytes. The buffer you asked for stays. The garbage you didn't, leaves.

When I'd skip it

If you already hoist the encoded bytes into a static readonly byte[] once at startup, you've solved the per-call allocation too, and u8 only really buys you clarity and the guarantee that it's truly static data rather than a heap array someone could mutate. The place u8 earns its keep is exactly the trap I fell into: GetBytes on a string literal sitting inside a hot loop, where it looks harmless and quietly isn't.

And it only works for literals the compiler can see. The moment your bytes come from a runtime string (a header value, a user's name, anything built while the program runs), you're back to GetBytes, as you should be. u8 is for the constants: delimiters, protocol framing, fixed JSON keys you write to a Utf8JsonWriter, the "HTTP/1.1 " kind of thing. My honest opinion is that Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("some literal") should read as a small code smell at this point — if the argument is a quoted constant, there's almost always a u8 that does it for free.

Since I hit a snag pushing this one to the repo, here's the whole measured sample inline — a net10.0 console app, dotnet run -c Release and it prints the table above:

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text;

const int Records = 2_000_000;
byte[] payload = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("{\"id\":42,\"ok\":true}");

long WriteWithGetBytes()
{
    using var buffer = new MemoryStream(Records * 32);
    for (int i = 0; i < Records; i++)
    {
        buffer.Write(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("data: "));
        buffer.Write(payload);
        buffer.Write(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("\n\n"));
    }
    return buffer.Length;
}

long WriteWithU8()
{
    using var buffer = new MemoryStream(Records * 32);
    for (int i = 0; i < Records; i++)
    {
        buffer.Write(Framing.Prefix);
        buffer.Write(payload);
        buffer.Write(Framing.Suffix);
    }
    return buffer.Length;
}

long Measure(string name, Func<long> run, int reps)
{
    long checksum = run();            // warm up
    GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();

    long bestMs = long.MaxValue;
    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    int g0 = GC.CollectionCount(0);
    for (int r = 0; r < reps; r++)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        checksum = run();
        sw.Stop();
        if (sw.ElapsedMilliseconds < bestMs) bestMs = sw.ElapsedMilliseconds;
    }
    double mb = (GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before) / (double)reps / (1024 * 1024);
    Console.WriteLine($"{name,-22} best {bestMs,4} ms {mb,7:F1} MB/pass gen0={GC.CollectionCount(0) - g0} (checksum {checksum})");
    return checksum;
}

Console.WriteLine($"Framing {Records:N0} records, best of 5 passes each\n");
long a = Measure("GetBytes per write", WriteWithGetBytes, 5);
long b = Measure("u8 literal", WriteWithU8, 5);
Console.WriteLine("\n" + (a == b ? "checksums match" : "MISMATCH"));

static class Framing
{
    public static ReadOnlySpan<byte> Prefix => "data: "u8;
    public static ReadOnlySpan<byte> Suffix => "\n\n"u8;
}

Anyone else have a GetBytes call hiding in a loop they forgot about? Go grep your hot paths for a quoted string argument — I bet you find one.

— still chasing allocations nobody asked me to chase

articles.title: Dark factory in two sentences
articles.description: Keboola Connection still has part of the system running on Zend Framework 1, the rest is already in Symfony. We're trying to cut that old part out, as much and as fast as we can. A short prompt was enough: in about 22 hours, 13 pull requests were ...
articles.body_html:
Keboola Connection still has part of the system running on Zend Framework 1, the rest is already in Symfony. We're trying to cut that old part out, as much and as fast as we can. A short prompt was enough: in about 22 hours, 13 pull requests were merged. Three more are open. And it can keep going for as long as any Zend remains in Connection.

A factory with the lights off

A dark factory, sometimes called a lights-out factory, is a manufacturing term for production that can run with almost no people on the shop floor. The lights can stay off because nobody has to stand at the line. Machines take in material, they manufacture, and a finished piece comes out the other end. A person built the line first, set the rules, and then shows up mainly when something needs maintenance, a quality check, or an intervention. Very few factories actually run like this around the clock with no people at all. As an idea, though, it fits.

And that's exactly what this experiment is about. Not whether an agent can remove Zend in one shot. Whether a solid harness can give you a line that runs on its own. Once you have that, a short prompt is enough.

All I had to write was this 

Your goal is to get as much of the Zend out of Connection as you can. You have until Friday.

Work in worktrees, use the skills in the repo for removing Zend, and don't open too many PRs at once, so we can keep up with merging them.

That's the whole brief. No long plan, no drip-feeding tasks from my side. The goal and the deadline: as much Zend gone as possible by Friday. The rest is guardrails. Each agent in its own worktree, so they don't step on each other. Use the skills that are already in the repo. And don't flood us with PRs, because we still have to get them merged.

The prompt doesn't say how a task is taken all the way to merge, that every PR should be tested with end-to-end tests, how merging to master works, what still needs to be cut away, or which gate is satisfied by a bot approval and which one wants a human. All of that is already in the setup. That's why two sentences are enough. Without what's underneath, it would just be a bold message in a chat window.

The map matters more than the skill

The last piece in there is a skill called migrate-highway. The skill itself isn't all that important. What matters is the map that comes with it.

It says which files in the modern part of the application still depend on the old one. What has to be cut out, rewritten, reformatted, have constants converted, and so on. I generated the map once with help from AI. Now AI rewrites it and a script checks it. The agent doesn't have to rediscover it at the start. It has a map, picks the next piece from it, and moves on.

I removed 56 dependencies from the new codebase on the old one.

From Linear to merge

Around that map we still have the same skills as in the setup. ship-task takes a task from Linear and gets it to just before merge. The gates are described in the skills. Some things can be merged on a bot approval alone. Some need a human review.

So it isn't just "here's a file, rewrite it". The agent picks up the work from Linear and sees it through. Every PR follows the same path: draft, E2E, the ai-review label, switching to ready, and joining the merge queue. One agent per git worktree.

On top of that we have skills for E2E tests, watching PRs and review threads, pre-commit checks, and endpoint migration.

When the gates say a bot is enough, it can go on without a human. When they say a human review is needed, it waits. Once a person approves, it merges automatically. The human hasn't left the line. They still approve what human review requires. They just don't have to stand at every step and push the work forward by hand.

BTW, we didn't build this harness for this one experiment. I described what the setup looks like for us in Everyone has better models. Why do some teams fly while others don't?. Here I just pointed it at one clear goal and let it run.

13 PRs in 22 hours

The main Claude Code session is the organizer. It starts subagents, they take care of the specific tasks, and it only checks whether they met all the conditions for a merge to master. And they go, and go, and go, until the goal is met.

I just tried it. In about 22 hours, 13 PRs were merged, three are open, 16 in total. One of the open ones is already in the merge queue, two are waiting for approval, and one of those still has E2E running after a rebase. Nothing is stuck.

The median from open to merge is about two hours. The fastest PR was done in 57 minutes. The ones that went out overnight waited 10 to 13 hours for review. One PR took 5.7 hours because of a long E2E queue and a bug fix.

The merged changes were small. Roles, quoting, admin features, a component detail, a table profile, a metadata fix, a metadata contract, a UI app detail, an event application, decomposing a string ID, dead Zend views, a table metadata list, constants for a file storage provider.

Two things slow it down the most: the E2E queue and waiting for human approvals. Single-suite runs line up in the queue with other runs, and the wait is typically 30 to 90 minutes. On some PRs the reviewer bot comes back with needs_human. And once a review is sitting with a person, the agent does not ask again, those are the rules.

Twice it kicked off E2E before the PR image was built, and once with the wrong filter. It fixed that itself. One mistake: it picked a candidate from a stale local main, and that piece was already done in a merged PR. All that was lost was the agent's time. Since then it picks candidates from origin/master.

Those 70 remaining actions won't get done without a human, that's true. But the Zend dependencies are going down, and the line keeps running overnight. Pretty cool.

How far do you let an agent run unattended? And what do your merge gates look like — can a bot approve, or does a human always have to sign off?

articles.title: Monuments of India, Part 2: Domes, Arches, Realistic Stone and Finer Details in three.js
articles.description: Last time, I proudly showed you 101 Indian monuments built entirely from code. This time I have to...
articles.body_html:
Last time, I proudly showed you 101 Indian monuments built entirely from code. This time I have to confess something: some of them were, let's say, enthusiastic approximations. That story is in I Built 101 Indian Monuments in the Browser Using Only Code.

Qutub Minar was wearing a cupola it never owned. The Taj Mahal had a lovely tomb but no actual garden. Dilwara had one temple where there should have been five. And a few of my buildings had a gorgeous front and, behind it, a back that looked like I'd lost interest halfway.

So I went on a fixing spree. Real doorways and guard niches on the forts. A proper charbagh for the Taj. Backs, sides and windows for the palaces. Towns that crowd around the temples like they've been there for centuries. Stone that catches the light, with veining, weathering and pietra dura. And yes, trees: the right trees. No more mango trees in the Thar Desert. Khejri and babul have been called in.

It is still 101 monuments in three.js, still pure code, and still not a single 3D model file downloaded. Come see what got more real, and help me spot what still looks like it's fibbing about its age.

Live: monuments-of-india-nu.vercel.app ·

Code: github.com/amananandrai/monuments-of-india

If the models or the code are useful to you, or you just like them, please give a star to the GitHub repo and help other people find the project.

TL;DR

  • The masses were already right. The joinery was not. Domes, screens, doors, backs of buildings and the ground around them got a second pass, monument by monument.
  • Shared parts for the family, detail files for the building. One dome, one jali, one gopuram for everyone, plus a file per monument for what only that monument has.
  • Everything is still code. Plain files and three.js, no build step, no model files, 650,000 triangles at most on a desktop and 300,000 on a phone.

In this post

  1. What changed since part 1
  2. How a part gets into a building
  3. Domes · Kiosks and turrets · Pillars and columns
  4. Arches, doors and windows · Eaves, battlements and bands
  5. Temple towers · Forts and monasteries
  6. When the shared kit is not the building
  7. What stands around the building
  8. Stone that catches the light
  9. How I checked the work, and what went wrong
  10. What I would still not claim · Add your own monument

What changed since part 1

This is the second pass, with the pictures from the component guides. The masses were already right. Up close, a dome was still a bare bulb, a screen was still a square grid, and the ground around a building was often the wrong trees or the wrong water. The work since then fills in the joinery, gives a few monuments pieces that only they have, and plants each site with what actually stands there.

Here is the short version, in the order I did it:

  • Real entrances. Forts got passages, guard niches and doors spiked against elephants. Temples got stepped doorways and porches. Mughal tombs got iwans and arcades.
  • A detail file for every monument, so a building has its own finer architecture and its own setting, not just a generic kit.
  • Photograph reviews. I compared the models with photographs in batches and fixed what disagreed: the Taj, Charminar, the Lotus Temple, the Hawa Mahal and many more.
  • Corrections. Qutub Minar lost the cupola it never had and gained Smith's Folly. The Taj Mahal got its full four-quarter charbagh. Dilwara got its other four temples.
  • Backs, sides and windows for palaces, mosques and tombs, so you can orbit them without finding a blank wall.
  • Towns and water around the temples at Kedarnath, Tirumala, Trimbak, Varanasi and Ujjain, plus the Old City round Charminar.
  • The right trees and the right water, per site.
  • Surfaces: photo textures with normal and roughness maps, calligraphy, pietra dura, carved reliefs and banded masonry.
  • Performance: monuments load when you open them, shadows follow the view, and phones get a lighter build.

Before and after

Same monument, same site, rendered by the same code: the left side is the repository before the second pass began, the right side is today.

Qutub Minar. The old tower wore a cupola it never owned. Now it tapers to its real top, and Smith's Folly, the Alai Darwaza, the cloister and Iltutmish's tomb stand around it, on grass with a path and trees.

Taj Mahal. The old tomb stood alone on a red plinth. Now it has its pishtaqs, calligraphy, chhatris and a charbagh garden to walk down.

Dilwara. One temple became the whole group of five, each in its own walled court, among trees.

Jaisalmer. A smooth sandstone mound with a ring wall became a fort at its real size on its Trikuta hill, with bastions, the road up to the gate and a town inside the walls.

Hawa Mahal. A flat stepped front with no depth became a screen of carved jharokhas, with the court and ranges behind it, the street in front and the building's sides finished.

The pictures below are the ones in components.md. node tools/shoot-components.mjs draws each shared part alone, in plain light. On the site the same part carries shadows, a photo texture and weathering. What each function takes, and which file it lives in, is in architecture.md and realism.md.

The site is still plain files and three.js, with no build step.

How a part gets into a building

Each monument has two files.

  • js/monuments/<name>.js builds the masses: plinth, walls, towers, roofs.
  • js/details/<name>.js adds the finer architecture and the setting, from addDetails(f, g).

f is the group the home view frames. g is the whole site, so a river or a town can sit outside the frame and not pull the camera back.

A few rules hold for every part:

  • Metres, y up. A part stands on y = 0 and faces +z unless its comment says otherwise.
  • The stone is passed in. M.marble, M.red, M.granite and the rest live in js/helpers.js. A one-off stone is mat('#hex', roughness).
  • Merge when the part is done. mergeByMaterial(group) leaves one mesh per material, so a facade of hundreds of small pieces is a handful of draw calls.
  • Two faces never share a plane. An overlay sits 2 to 5 cm off its wall. node check-flicker.mjs <id> from tools/ finds the ones that do not.

Placing a row of windows is a loop around the four faces:

// A window on each face, 11 m out from the centre, the sill 13.6 m up.
for (const a of FACES) {
  d.add(onFace(at(windowFrame(2, 4.2, M.cream, { shape: 'flat' }), 0, 13.6, 0), a, 11.01));
}

at moves a part. onFace turns that move onto a wall: angle 0 is the +z face, the next number is how far out, and a third number walks along the face. aroundCircle and alongFace do the same for a ring of brackets or a cornice. Hundreds of identical merlons or columns go through inst(), one geometry drawn many times.

Domes

A dome is rarely just a dome. The bulb springs from a drum through a moulded neck, and the finial that crowns it tells you the tradition: a Mughal spike, a temple pot, a crescent.
Onion dome: neck, lotus crown, finial Lotus dome: ribs, a cup of petals, a crescent

onionDome(r, m) is a lathe of the shared onion profile. From 1.5 m radius upward (4 m on a phone) it adds two more lathes that ride on the same group, so moving, scaling or ribbing the dome carries them along:

export function onionDome(r, m, {
  crown = r >= (detail.low ? 4 : 1.5),
  neck = r >= (detail.low ? 4 : 1.5),
} = {}) {
  const o = lathe(ONION.map(([a, b]) => [a * r, b * r]), m, 48);
  if (neck) o.add(lathe(DOME_NECK.map(([a, b]) => [a * r, b * r]), m, 32));
  if (crown) o.add(ribbed(lathe(DOME_CROWN.map(([a, b]) => [a * r, b * r]), m, 32), 16, 0.1));
  return o;
}

The neck is the moulding where the bulb springs from the drum. The crown is the inverted lotus, sixteen ribs pressed in by ribbed(), which is the mahapadma the finial rises from. { crown: false } or { neck: false } leaves one off where a monument models its own. The Taj does.

Around that sit the other turned shapes: hemi for a plain hemisphere, persianDome for a pointed double curve, lotusDome for an onion with shallow ribs sitting in a cup of petals, petalRing for the petals themselves, and finial, kalash and crescentFinial for whatever crowns it. A temple pot, a Mughal spike and a crescent are three different functions, because they are three different objects.

Kiosks and turrets

The chhatri, a small domed kiosk on columns, is the silhouette of Rajput and Mughal skylines. Take them off a roofline and it stops looking like India.
Chhatri Mughal chhatri Guldastas
Minaret Jharokha

chhatri(r, h, m, domeM) is the domed kiosk on eight columns that stands on Mughal and Rajput roofs. At full detail each column gets a moulded base and a spreading capital, the eave gets a drip edge, and the dome sits on a low drum. mughalChhatri is the richer one: arches between the columns, a sloping eave, a ribbed lotus dome, and an optional crescent.

guldasta is the Lucknow roof turret, a thin shaft under a tiny onion and a spike. minaret tapers, takes a list of balconies, and is capped by a chhatri. jharokha is the oriel on brackets, screened on three sides, under a roof that can be curved Bengal ('bangla'), domed, or flat. banglaRoof is that curve on its own, for pavilions as well as windows.

Pillars and columns

Classical, plain and Corinthian Carved temple pillar Cluster pillar
Yali pillar Column trim on bare shafts

These are different orders, so they are different functions.

  • column(r, h, m, { order }) in js/details/colonial.js is a classical column: plinth, base, tapering shaft, capital. order: 'corinthian' adds flutes and acanthus. entablature and corinthianCapital are what a colonnade carries above it.
  • carvedPillar is a temple pillar: square base, octagonal shaft with two carved bands, a cushion and a capital.
  • clusterPillar is the Vijayanagara pillar, a shaft ringed by slender colonnettes. yaliPillar carries a rearing yali and its rider. Both are sculpted rather than stacked from boxes.
  • columnTrim(list, m, { capM }) dresses a colonnade that was built as bare instanced shafts: a plinth and moulding under each, a necking ring and an abacus at the head. It is on Agra Fort's Diwan-i-Am, the Padmanabhaswamy corridor, Mahakaleshwar's colonnade and the Secretariat loggias at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
  • pilasters are the flat ones, proud of a wall by a few centimetres.

The trim matters because the cheap way to draw forty columns is one instanced cylinder. That reads as a row of poles. Bases and capitals are a second instanced pass, so the shafts stay cheap and the order comes back.

Arches, doors and windows

Arch and its ring Iwan Niche
Window with a jali Classical door Gothic window
Temple doorway

archWall cuts an opening through a wall. archRing is the moulded band around it. niche is a blind arch with a half-dome hood, deep enough to read as a recess. iwan, in js/details/mughal.js, is the great recessed arch of a gate or a tomb front, with its door. arcadeSkin cuts a wall into a row of arched cells, each a door, a screen or a room. mughalDoorway is the smaller pointed door onto a dim interior.

The traditions that are not Mughal have their own doors, because a fanlight is not a torana.

  • templeDoorway is a stepped frame, a hood, timber leaves standing open, a lamp in the sanctum, and guardians. doorLeaves can take spikes, the iron points set against war elephants. doorFrame is the nested carved bands of a post-and-lintel door. interior is the dim room seen through it. templePorch is the small open porch in front.
  • classicalDoor, porch and pediment are the colonial and Indo-Saracenic set. gothicDoor, gothicWindow and oculus are the pointed portal, the two-light window and the round window.
  • windowFrame(w, h, m, { shape, screen }) is a window in a stone surround. screen: jali(m) fills it.

The jali, from a grid to a lattice

A jali is a pierced stone screen. It lets air and light through while keeping a room private, and it is one of the most recognisable things in Mughal and Rajput architecture. It is also the part that used to be a square grid. It is now the octagon-and-diamond lattice of Mughal and Rajput screens, one function for the cut and the shading so they cannot drift apart. A 22 cm grid:

float sJaliHole(vec2 uv) {
  vec2 p = abs(fract(uv / 0.22) - 0.5);
  float oct = step(max(p.x, p.y), 0.34) * step(p.x + p.y, 0.47);
  float dia = step(1.0 - p.x - p.y, 0.13);
  return max(oct, dia);
}

Up close, when the holes are large enough on screen not to shimmer, the shader discards the opening. The stone around it still casts the shadow. Far away the lattice stays a shading pattern. Modelling every hole on 101 buildings was never going to fit the triangle budget: 650,000 on a desktop, 300,000 on a phone.

The same trick covers the ornament that should stay cheap: frieze for a band of rosettes, carved(m, kind) for 'script', 'calligraphy', 'pietra', 'reliefs' and 'tiles', plus rosette, medallion, sunburst and lettering for the roundels and the raised names. The pattern lives in the shader. The mesh stays a wall.

Eaves, battlements and bands

Chhajja on brackets Merlons Railing

chhajja is the deep sloping eave. chhajjaRing is the round version. bracketGeo is the corbel that carries an eave or a balcony, and placeAll drops one copy at every point in a list. merlons is a row of pointed battlements. On a fort, rampart and bastionCrowns add the parapet, a string course and arrow slits, for a long curtain wall and for round bastions.

railing and railingRing are posts with pierced screens between them. balustrade is the classical version. beltCourse runs a band around a rectangular building, mouldings stacks courses into a plinth or a cornice, dentils is the row of small blocks under that cornice, and panel is a sunk field that can be carved or inlaid. wallWithGaps is a compound wall with openings left for its gates.

Temple towers

Shikhara Nagara temple Dravida vimana
Gopuram Mandap Temple niche

nagaraTemple({ w, h, m, halls, … }) builds a North Indian temple in one call: sanctum, curved spire, and halls stepping out in front. That is why Somnath, in the first article, fits under 1 KB. shikhara is the spire alone, with nagaraProfile and kalingaProfile as two tapers. bhumijaRows sets miniature spires between the bands of a Bhumija tower.

dravidaVimana is the stepped tower over a South Indian sanctum. Each storey's edge carries miniature shrines: kuta at the corners, shala along the sides, laid out by haraRow. gopuram(w, d, h, tiers, seed) is the gate tower, tier on tier of painted stucco figures. The seed is why Meenakshi's towers are not copies of each other. mandap is a pillared hall under a stepped roof. storeyedHall stacks galleries. pidaRoof is the stepped pyramid of slabs on its own.

templeNiche(w, h, m, { figure }) puts an image in a niche. For a long row, idol is the cheap standing figure in relief. trabeateGate is a post-and-lintel gatehouse, with guardians or carved beasts. dwajasthambha is the gold flagstaff in front of the sanctum. grandStair is the broad flight between side walls, with a landing and guardians.
Grand stair Figure frieze Statue, urn, pinnacle

figure, guardian, statue and figureFrieze are the sculpted ones. The great statues, Patel, Bahubali, Thiruvalluvar and the Nageshwar Shiva, are each one continuous skin, grown from a signed distance field in js/sdf.js and meshed in the browser, so a limb grows out of a body the way it does in a carving.

The temples got the biggest structural rethink in this pass. Ram Mandir now has three storeys with cusped arches and a 32-step stair. Somnath's spire rises in seven storeys over a three-tier plinth and a broad stair. Mahakaleshwar has three storeys of shrines under its spire. The shared parts that made this cheap, grandStair, storeyedHall and the cusped arch, are now available to every temple.

Forts and monasteries

Fort gate Rampart and bastion Monks' houses
Dharma wheel and victory banner

fortGate is a gatehouse with a real passage, guard niches, and leaves spiked against elephants. towerDetail adds string courses and arrow slits to a round tower. slitRow is a row of slits along a wall.

A gate that is only an arch painted on a wall reads as scenery. A passage you could walk reads as a fort.

For the Himalayan monasteries, tibetanBlock is the whitewashed mass with dark windows under a maroon band. quarters dresses a list of those blocks as monks' houses: windows in black surrounds, doors, beam ends, earth roofs, prayer-flag poles. dharmaWheel is the gilded wheel between two deer over an assembly hall. gyaltsen is the victory banner at a roof corner, shabkhep the pleated awning over a window, parapetDiscs the gilded discs along a parapet. tibetanDoor and tibetanPortico are the painted door and the pillared porch.

The ground under a hill monastery comes from js/details/terrain.js: heightField shapes a surface from a height function, rock where it is steep, scrub or grass where it is not, and mountainRing sets a ring of mountains around a valley. That is how Tawang sits on its spur, Kailasa is cut out of a basalt escarpment, Ajanta sits in its horseshoe gorge, and Amber stands on its ridge with Jaigarh's wall above.

When the shared kit is not the building

Shared parts get a monument into the right family. They do not make the Taj the Taj. The detail file is where a photograph would disagree with a generic kit.

The Taj Mahal. Each face is a pishtaq: a deep pointed arch in a rectangular frame, roofed by a half-dome, with calligraphy in black marble and inlaid flowers in the spandrels. Smaller arched alcoves with pierced screens sit either side. The parapet carries leaf-shaped merlons, the drum a blind arcade, and the four roof chhatris have arches, an eave and a lotus cap. The minarets take three bracketed balconies. The dome's own lotus is modelled here, so the shared crown stays off. And around it all lies the charbagh, the four-quarter garden that the first version forgot.

Konark. The Sun Temple is a stone chariot, so the plinth is wrapped in friezes of elephants and daily life, above and below the wheels. The Jagamohana stands on carved mouldings, with an image in a niche either side of each doorway. At the steps of the Natamandira, lions rear over elephants. The horses are sculpted.

Hawa Mahal. Each jharokha of the screen projects on a pair of small carved brackets under the sill. The white lime bands along the storeys are carved. A lotus crowns each domed kiosk. Flowering bougainvillea sits at either end of the pavement. The lattice holes stay in the shader, so the stone is still solid and the screens still cast shadows. Behind the screen there is now a court, with ranges and ramps, so the building is no longer a facade with nothing behind it.

India Gate, Charminar, the Taj, the Gateway of India and the Old Parliament House carry the most of this layer: roundels, lettering, nested arches, bracketed balconies, jalis, eaves, merlons, lotus domes. The others take the carving of their own tradition. Base mouldings and image niches on the temples. Banded bastions and jharokhas on the forts. Stacked iwans and inlaid stars on the Mughal tombs. Capitals, balustrades and eaves on the colonial buildings.

What stands around the building

Everything that is not the monument comes from js/details/realism.js, with the animals in js/details/animals.js. A part takes a list of spots, [x, z] in metres. Variation comes from a seed, so a visit looks the same as the last one. copies() instances the shape and marks it as dressing, which the home view ignores when it frames the building. Fifty trees are a few draw calls.

Twenty-one kinds of tree, one planter

Broadleaf Wide Dry
Columns and conifers Palms Shrubs

trees(spots, { kind, seed, y, h }) plants every kind. One table, KINDS, holds the default height, the plain crown, the full crown, the leaf and the bark. An unknown kind throws, naming itself. Only the banyan drops aerial roots. Six silhouettes cover the twenty-one: a broadleaf, a wide broadleaf, a dry umbrella, a column, a tiered conifer, and the palm.

Where What stands there
Delhi's avenues Jamun
Bodh Gaya and Sarnath Peepal, the bodhi tree
Kashmir Chinar, pale, on a thick trunk
Ladakh, by the Indus Poplar and willow
Tawang and Rumtek Fir
Ajanta, and the forests Teak and sal
The south Tamarind
Konark and the Shore Temple Casuarina behind the palms
Jaisalmer, Chittorgarh, the dry ridges Khejri, dhok, babul, ber 
// Twelve jamun down each side of a path. The seed keeps this avenue the same on every visit.
g.add(trees(
  [...along(12, [-58, 14], [-58, 185]), ...along(12, [58, 14], [58, 185])],
  { kind: 'jamun', seed: 6 }
));

along is an avenue. scatter fills a rectangle and stays out of the building. around is a ring.

Every tree starts as a trunk and one crown. That is all a phone keeps. On a desktop, upgradeTrees() replants that monument's trees with a leaning trunk, limbs, and separate leaf clumps, smallest planting first, for as long as the model stays inside its triangle budget. Palms grow fronds with leaflets. Deodars grow drooping tiers. Six specimen trees become full trees. A forest of 160 usually stays plain. Each tree also takes one of three forms of its kind, so a row is not a row of clones.

shrubs has three readings. Plain is a clipped green bush. dry: true is the grey-green scrub of a dry hill. flowers: '#d0306f' is a dark bush with a smaller muted cap, bougainvillea or marigold, deliberately not a bush made entirely of bloom.

Lamps, flags, boats, towns

Lamps, bench, bollards ASI board Fountains
Prayer flags Tricolour and pennant Marigold garlands

lampPosts are fluted iron posts with a scrolled arm and a glass lantern, lit at night. asiBoard is the blue board on two posts. fountains rise and fall into a ring of foam. umbrellas are the cane and cloth shades on bamboo poles. prayerFlags run from point to point in the five colours. garland hangs marigold strands, orange and yellow. flag is a rippling pennant, saffron or the Nishan Sahib. tricolour is the national flag with the Ashoka Chakra.
Country boats Ferry launches Cargo ship
Houseboats Stalls Town houses

boats, launches, ships and houseboats take a water height, so a boat floats on its lake. stalls stand outside temple gates and in Laad Bazaar at Charminar. townHouses builds two to five storeys with windows, doors and shop signs. tanks is the share of flat roofs that carry a black water tank, 0.7 by default and 0.15 in the fort town at Jaisalmer. cityAround lines streets on every side of a rectangle and leaves the roads in keep open. At Puri, two rows of houses stand outside Jagannath's outer wall, and the Grand Road stays clear.

Towns are the change I like most. Kedarnath has its pilgrim town along the stone path. Tirumala has the temple town round its Mada streets. Varanasi's old city wraps the Kashi Vishwanath corridor, and Ujjain's old town sits beyond Mahakaleshwar. The Gateway of India has Elephanta ferry launches and ships at anchor.
Traffic on the two bridges that have it

traffic runs only on the Howrah Bridge and the Bandra–Worli Sea Link. There are no motor vehicles anywhere else, and no people at all, so the monument stays the subject.

Animals

Nandi Elephants Horse and lion
Deer Yaks and camels

nandi sits before a Shiva temple. elephant can be stone or bronze. rideElephant adds cloth and a howdah. lion is a gate guardian, and the Lion Capital. deer stand at Sarnath and Sikandra. yaks are in the mountains. camels wear saddle cloths in the Thar. horse, scaled down, is the ponies at Kedarnath. The larger animals are one continuous skin, heavier than the rest of the kit, and the slowest of them are meshed while the map sits idle.

Ground, water, and the shade at a wall's foot

The first scenery was generous, and often invented. Mango and coconut stood in the desert. Pools sat where the ground is grass. A lawn ended like a tile.

Water was put back where the site has it, and taken out where it had been added. The Tungabhadra runs north of Hampi's Vittala compound, palms on its bank. A stone-rimmed lotus pond lies south of the Mahabodhi railing. The Shahi Baoli stands east of the Bara Imambara, a walled stepwell through an arched gate. Ramappa's lake lies beyond the temple garden. India Gate lost the canals at its piers. Jallianwala Bagh's flame stands on the grass. Rameswaram's sea sits east of the temple, in the town. Maota Lake at Amber mirrors the fort.

Paths are flagstones. Courses are 70 cm deep, stones are 1.1 m long, every third course is half-length, and the courses shift so no joint runs straight through. Each stone has its own tone. Far off, the joints drop away and the floor stays slightly mottled.

float row = floor(uv.y / 0.7);
float wdt = mod(row, 3.0) < 0.5 ? 0.55 : 1.1;
float xo = uv.x + row * 0.37;

A wall meets the grass in shade, not in a hard line. When a monument is shown, it is drawn once from straight above into a 512×512 height map (groundShade in js/surface.js). Upward faces darken where that blur stands well above them. Trees are left out of the pass, because they already cast shadows. It runs on phones too.

Ceremonial lawns stay mown: India Gate, the Taj, Victoria, the National War Memorial, both Parliaments. Elsewhere, desktops get grass tufts under about 0.35 m, kept 4 m clear of the monument and off any path.

Close to a building, the camera casts a ray toward its target. If it has entered a solid it steps back out, and it keeps about 1.5 m off a wall in front of it. The home view frames the monument, not the lawns around it, and fifteen monuments open on the view of their best-known photograph: the Taj down its garden, the Red Fort's Lahori Gate, Meenakshi's south gopuram, Hawa Mahal's street front.

At night, floodlights and festival lights come on and stars fill the sky. Press the Night button on any monument to see it.

Stone that catches the light

The shader still paints joints, veins, brick courses, weathering and a slight tint per piece, from world position, so nothing has to be unwrapped. A one-metre block is the same size on the Qutub Minar as on the walls of Agra Fort. Over that, most stones carry a CC0 photograph from Poly Haven: marble, red and cream sandstone, granite, laterite, dark coursed blocks, fort rubble, plaster, lime, khondalite, concrete and weathered planks.
Marble Red sandstone Granite

Each set has a normal map and a roughness map beside the colour, packed by tools/pack-textures.py. On a desktop the shader projects them the same way as the colour, so the stone catches the light as a rough surface. Phones keep the colour map. A set is fetched the first time a monument that uses it is opened, not all of them at startup.

On top of the stone comes the ornament. The Taj gets black calligraphy bands round its pishtaqs. Itmad-ud-Daulah gets pietra dura over its walls, towers and pavilion. CSMT gets buff stone coursed with blue-grey basalt. Rani ki Vav gets sculpted panels on its side walls. All of it lives in the shader, so the mesh stays a wall.

Shadows follow the view. The shadow map used to cover a fixed box around the whole monument, so on a large site one texel was most of a metre. It now stays about three-quarters of the camera's distance from its target, changes in steps so the shadows do not crawl, and is redrawn only when a step is crossed. Desktops start at full sharpness and step down for that visit if the frame rate cannot hold.

On a phone, below 760 px wide, ambient occlusion and reflections are skipped. Trees stay plain, the ground has no tufts, towns and traffic are thinned, and the heavier carving waits. ?detail=high or ?detail=low on the address chooses.

How I checked the work, and what went wrong

Procedural models fail in a particular way: they look fine from the home view and wrong from two metres away. So most of the second pass was checking.

  • Photograph reviews. I went through the monuments in batches and compared each model with photographs of the real building. That is how the Taj, Charminar, the Lotus Temple, Mahabodhi and the Hawa Mahal got their fixes, and how a handful of near-misses were found and closed.
  • Full audits. After the photo reviews I went round the whole set again, in groups: views and land forms, mountains and towns, then framing, missing pieces and flicker.
  • Headless checks. The scripts in tools/ run in Node and Playwright and check triangle budgets, heights, filters, flicker and detail counts. They stop a regression from hiding in monument number 87.

Things that went wrong along the way, as I found them:

  • Flicker. Two faces on the same plane fight over the pixel. Windows, glazing and sea were all guilty. check-flicker.mjs finds them, and the rule is now that an overlay sits 2 to 5 cm off its wall.
  • A dark seam at the foot of sculpted hills, where the land met the ground.
  • A black reflection pixel on the Bandra–Worli Sea Link.
  • Eleven models that were too tall for their real heights, brought back within them.
  • Water and trees that were simply invented. The first scenery was generous. The mango orchard in the desert was the most photogenic of the lot.

I also made some deliberate cuts. The jali holes are not modelled, because 101 buildings of them would never fit the triangle budget. People are not in the scenes, and motor vehicles appear only on the two bridges that have traffic, so the monument stays the subject.

What I would still not claim

These are interpretations, not survey records. The goal is that someone who knows the building can see its plan, its material and its setting, and that someone who does not can tell a gopuram from a shikhara, and Konark from a generic temple.

The rule from the second pass is small. Repeated joinery lives in one shared part, which is why the pictures above are a catalogue and not 101 separate models. The thing that makes a monument itself lives in that monument's file. The tree and the water are the ones the site's own notes name. A new dome profile does not need a new texture unwrap. A new tree is one row in KINDS.

If you know a building well and see something wrong, I would like to hear it. Open an issue with a photograph or a source, and it becomes the next fix.

Add your own monument

Adding another monument is still one module and one card in js/data.js.

  1. Create js/monuments/<name>.js with the masses: plinth, walls, towers, roofs.
  2. Add its card to js/data.js: name, place, dates, style, material and a few facts.
  3. Optionally add js/details/<name>.js with addDetails(f, g) for the finer architecture and the setting. Reuse the shared parts first.
  4. Run the checks in tools/ (budgets, heights, flicker). See tools/README.md.

The code is MIT licensed, so you are free to use it, learn from it and build on it.

Try it

  • Explore: monuments-of-india-nu.vercel.app. Open #taj-mahal, then #konark-sun-temple, #hawa-mahal and #jaisalmer-fort.
  • The guides, with every part: components, architecture, the setting, how it is drawn.
  • If you found this helpful, or you like the project, star the repo on GitHub.

Which building still looks least like itself? Tell me in the comments. That is the next detail file.

The component pictures are rendered from the repo by tools/shoot-components.mjs. The project's code is MIT licensed, and so is three.js. Photo textures are CC0 from Poly Haven. Map data is public domain from Natural Earth.

articles.title: Local AI models need to be a browser feature
articles.description: I started thinking about the Web Models API while experimenting with building AI-native GUIs. I was...
articles.body_html:
I started thinking about the Web Models API while experimenting with building AI-native GUIs. I was exploring the idea of UI as a function of AI: the model would generate the content and choose the component best suited to display it.

One experiment was a news site which used LLMs to identify key topics (people, places, or things) in an article and turn those topics into links. A reader could click on a topic to get more context, presented in a component suited to that content.

While working on demos I kept running into the same problem. Running an LLM in the browser with WebAssembly or WebGPU meant having the app load and run the model itself, and the performance wasn't good enough for what I was building. Using a cloud provider meant paying for usage, even when I just wanted to share a demo.

That got me thinking about what this means for indie developers. Putting an experiment or small product online can mean an ongoing bill before you know whether anyone finds it useful or have a way to fund it.

I wanted web apps to use on-device models with the user's permission, much like asking to use a camera or microphone. This led me to build my first attempt at solving this. Browser.AI was a prototype that exposed an API on the window object to access models running on-device. The learnings from that became the foundation for the Web Models API proposal.

Web Models API — Models belong in every browser.

A proposed browser API for web apps that need a particular open-weight model. People control access; the browser runs it. Join the Web Models API discussion.

webmodels.dev

How it works

The Web Models API exposes access to open-weight on-device models through a simple verb oriented API on navigator.models. The app requests an open-weight model using a universal ID so developers can target the exact model release they built and tested against.

The user decides if a site can access that model, and at any point can revoke access. The permission is tied to the model and site pairing, so permission to use one model does not give the site access to every model on the device.

The browser sets up and runs models, manages resource use, and shares model weights across sites. Each app doesn't need their own copy of the model, but the data and permissions stay separate.

The API also supports tool calls, structured output, and multimedia. An app could provide functions for filtering a list, choosing a component, or updating a form; the model requests a function call, and the app checks it before running it. Structured output means the app gets back JSON it can render directly, not text it has to parse. Multimedia input means a model can take an image directly, useful for something like a receipt reader.

So for my news site experiment, the app would still decide what context to send, check the model's response, and render the selected component. The browser handles running the model.

Cost and control

When a suitable model can run on the user's device, you don't need a paid cloud inference service. For me, this is also about control: over where our money goes, and over where our users' data goes. Developers should be able to decide when paying a cloud provider adds value and when a local model is enough.

In many cases there's no good reason to send that data to a server when the same task can run securely on the user's machine. Someone filling out a tax form or discussing a medical scan shouldn't have to trust that data to a cloud provider when the device they're using can do the job.

There are also reasons to run locally beyond cost and privacy. A notes app could search personal documents without sending their contents to a model provider, and with the model, app, and documents available locally, that search works offline. Local processing also skips the network round trip.

Why model choice matters

I believe competitive open-weight models are an important part of that future. Different tasks need different models. A small model may be enough to choose a UI component. Document search needs an embedding model. A receipt reader needs a model that can handle images. Developers should be able to choose based on what works for their app, independently of which browser someone uses.
The Prompt API provides access to a browser specified language model. But apps often end up tuning their prompts to one model's quirks. Those prompts may work poorly in another browser or after a model update.

In my UI experiments, the model's ability to identify content and select the right component was part of how the app worked. A different model could make different choices. You'll run into the same issue if you want to use embeddings for document search: an app must use the same embedding model to index documents and later search them. Developers need a defined model target they can test, and a way to choose when to move to a new release.

Being forced to use the model a big tech company shipped with their browser makes us developers dependent on their internal business strategies. For example, if they decide that on-device inference is a challenge to their cloud business, they might be less motivated to improve the model. I want developers and users to have real alternatives, with less dependence on a few companies' pricing, model choices, and decisions about how their services work.

Help shape it

I care about this because I want to keep building and sharing useful and interesting applications of AI, and I want other developers to be able to do the same. Funding an expensive cloud inference bill and sending your users' data into a black box shouldn't be requirements to access AI, especially when the task can run on hardware the user already has.

The Web Models API is still early, and I'd like to hear from developers.

If you could run a specific open-weight model in any browser, for free, what would you build? Which model would you use? If you've already shipped AI features with Transformers.js, the Prompt API, or a cloud provider, what got in your way?

Let me know in the comments. The explainer and API reference are on Github if you want the details. In the next post, I'll walk through the API with code.

articles.title: A black box is not redaction — and three other things I got wrong building local PDF tools
articles.description: Take any PDF. Draw a black rectangle over a line of text in a viewer that lets you annotate. Save it....
articles.body_html:
Take any PDF. Draw a black rectangle over a line of text in a viewer that lets you annotate. Save it. Open it again and drag-select across the rectangle.

The text comes back.

That is the entire reason I built a PDF tool site, and it is also the first thing I got wrong.

A black box is a drawing, not a deletion

An annotation is an object layered on top of the page content. The characters underneath are still there, in the content stream, encoded exactly as they were before you covered them up. Select-all still finds them. Copy still copies them. Any text extractor still returns them.

Actual redaction means the characters stop existing in the file. Not hidden, not covered, not rendered white-on-white — gone from the content stream, so that extraction returns nothing.

I built the redaction tool around that distinction, and then I made the checker report a number instead of a picture. Counting characters inside the marked areas turns out to be the only way to tell a real deletion from a good-looking one.

Three different zeros

This is the part that took me longest to get right, and it is the part most redaction tools skip.

If the checker says "0 characters inside the marked areas," that sentence can mean three completely different things:

  1. The text is gone. The page had a text layer, you marked it, and now extraction returns 0. This is the result you want, and the report calls it CLEARED.
  2. There was never a text layer. The page is a scan. Every pixel is an image; there are no characters to find in the first place. The tool reports NOTHING TO MEASURE, because the 0 is the absence of a measurement, not a clean result. A scanner output can look identical to a properly redacted page and mean the opposite thing — one has no text because it never did, the other has no text because you removed it.
  3. You drew the box on empty space. Same 0, same false comfort. The text you meant to remove is three lines down.

The first version of my checker merged all three into a single "0" with a green tick. That is a security product telling you what you want to hear. The current version reports the source page's character count next to the output's, so a scan and a clean redaction can never look the same.

There is a fourth result, and it is the ugly one: the marked page still hands back extractable text after processing. The report says so in plain words and tells you to treat the output like the original. It has happened in testing. I would rather the tool say that than round up to success.

What actually happens to the file

The redaction runs locally: the page is rendered to a canvas at 2× (about 144 DPI), the marked pages are rebuilt as JPEGs at quality 0.9, and the result is assembled into a new PDF. Pages you did not mark are copied through with their original text layer intact.

That has a consequence the tool states on the report rather than hides: a rebuilt page is an image, so everything on it stops being selectable — including the text that was not inside a box. If you need the rest of the page to stay searchable, you cannot have that and a destroyed text layer on the same page. Pick which one matters for this document.

The leak nobody looks at

Redaction is about what is visible. Metadata is about what is attached.

I stripped Title, Author, Subject and friends, and the file still carried the old title. The cause: pdf-lib removes the catalog's reference to the XMP packet, but the packet itself survives as an unreferenced indirect object inside the document. Delete the pointer and the body stays.

The second mistake was the check. I searched the output bytes for x:xmpmeta and found nothing, so I called it clean. The object was compressed. A byte search over a deflated stream tells you nothing at all — and this is exactly the kind of false pass that makes a verification step worse than no verification step.

The fix was to enumerate every indirect object after stripping, decompress each stream (UTF-8 first, then deflate, then raw deflate), and count the ones that still contain an XMP packet. Streams over 5 MB are reported as unscanned rather than silently skipped, because "I did not check this" and "this is clean" are different answers.

On my test file: 1,634 bytes in, 766 out, no XMP left. Compressed variant: 1,256 to 754.

Two more surprises, both about what tools quietly drop

Rebuilding a PDF is a destructive operation and the destructive part is not always where you expect.

PDFDocument.create() plus copyPages does not carry Author, Title or XMP into the new document — so a merge tool built this way produces a file with the contents of both inputs and the metadata of neither. It also stamps its own Producer and Creator as pdf-lib (...). If you were merging to preserve a document's provenance, you did not.

Same for splitting: each part is a fresh document, so each part arrives with no author and no title, whatever the original had. A tool page claiming otherwise is a page contradicting its own code.

The page-level limits are equally unglamorous: splitting one page per file caps at 50 pages, converting to JPG caps at 100, redaction caps at 50, and every tool caps the upload at 100 MB. These are browser limits, not policy — past that point memory pressure starts killing tabs, and a tool that crashes halfway is worse than one that refuses up front.

How to check that nothing is uploaded

This is the claim everything else rests on, so it should be falsifiable in ten seconds rather than taken on trust.

Open the tool, open the browser's Network tab, and drop a file in. You will see no request carrying your document. What you will see is static assets, and Cloudflare's analytics beacon, which the host injects into every page it serves — that is the CDN counting visits, not your file going anywhere. Clear the log, process the file, and watch it stay empty.

Five tools, all of them local

Everything above is implemented in the browser with pdf-lib and pdf.js. No server, no queue, no upload step, because there is nothing to upload to.

  • Redact a PDF without uploading it — draw boxes, rebuild the marked pages as images, get a report that separates the three zeros. Not a certification, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a compliance workflow that requires one.
  • Strip metadata from a PDF — Info dictionary and XMP, verified by decompressing every object rather than trusting the pointer deletion.
  • Merge PDFs in the browser — page contents carried, metadata deliberately not.
  • Split a PDF into single pages — one file per page or fixed ranges, zero-padded names so part10 sorts after part9 and not before part2.
  • Convert PDF pages to JPG — 144 or 216 DPI, quality 0.92 fixed, one download per page or a single ZIP.

Disclosure: these are my own tools. No affiliate links, nothing paid, no account required.

If you need redaction that survives opposing counsel, this is not that product, and I would rather say so here than in a support email. What it is: a local check you can run before you send a file you are not sure about.

articles.title: The job scanner that marked postings "done" without reading them
articles.description: career-ops is an open-source job-search tool with over 80,000 stars on GitHub. One part of it,...
articles.body_html:
career-ops is an open-source job-search tool with over 80,000 stars on GitHub. One part of it, openrouter-runner, takes the job postings in your pipeline, opens each page in a headless browser, sends the job text to a free model on OpenRouter, and writes a score into your tracker.

On 23 October I ran it on 15 live Workday postings (career-ops v1.37.0). All 15 rows were marked done. All 15 got a report.

Then I counted what the model had actually received.

What the model saw

Between 0 and 397 characters of job text per posting. Six of the 15 got nothing at all. The rest got the page frame, for example:

Skip to main content Loading Follow Us © 2026 Workday, Inc. All rights reserved.

That is 80 characters. No title, no requirements, no description.

The cause was one line. After opening the page, the runner waited a fixed 2 seconds, then read the body. Workday builds the job description with JavaScript after the page loads. When I reran the same postings the next day, the description appeared 5.0 to 9.2 seconds after navigation started, on 13 of the 15. Two seconds was never going to be enough.

Why "done" was the real bug

A slow page is normal. The bug was what happened next: the pipeline treated "the model replied" as "the posting was evaluated".

To show it without any real model, I pointed the runner at three local pages with no job text, and replaced the model with a stub that always answers Score: 4.2/5. All three went out with 0 characters of job text. All three were marked done. The tracker said 4.2/5 | Evaluated.

Nothing in the tracker separates a real score from a score about nothing. Someone reading it would apply, or skip, based on a number that came from an empty page.

A second bug in the same runner

The runner reuses the prompt that career-ops gives to agents that have tools. That prompt tells the model to search the web, run other scripts, check the CV. The runner sends no tools.

So the free models did what the prompt asked. On Workday pages with no description, 19 of 19 replies were tool calls, or said they were about to make one. On real descriptions (7.8K to 16K characters), 4 replies came back: 3 tool calls and 1 empty. Across all 23 replies, the score parser found 0 scores.

How it got fixed

I filed both bugs as issue #5809 on 24 October, with the numbers above and the stub script. Fixing it took four pull requests. Three are mine:

PR What changed Merged
#5814 (by bercedev) A posting that wasn't read is not saved or marked done 25 Oct
#5817 The runner tells the model it has no tools, and strips the steps it can't run 26 Oct
#6017 Model timeout raised from 15 s to 120 s 27 Oct
#6169 Wait for the job description, not for a fixed 2 s 6 Nov

6017 came out of the same work. The 15-second timeout was set in June, when the two prompt files the runner sends added up to about 31K characters. By October they were about 113K. On the free model rotation, a timeout also put the model on a blacklist that survives restarts.

After #5814, the false "done" was gone. But it showed the next problem: with the 2-second wait still there, a Workday posting could never be read, so its row stayed pending forever. I measured 20 live Workday postings, 4 each from NVIDIA, Salesforce, Adobe, Intel and Mastercard:

  • With the fixed 2 s wait: 0 of 20 readable. All refused as too short, in 3 to 4 seconds.
  • With a wait for the job text: 20 of 20 readable, 3,680 to 9,072 characters, in 3.3 to 6.9 seconds.

6169 first tries career-ops' own job-board API reader (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever and others), and only falls back to the browser if that returns nothing. In the browser it waits until the main content holds more than 1,500 visible characters, or until the page clearly says the posting is closed, with a 15-second cap. A 4xx or 5xx page skips the wait.

What review added

The maintainer asked for changes, and the automated reviewer (CodeRabbit) raised findings over several rounds. Not all of it was noise. One finding was real, and it came from my own change: a page with an "Apply now" button and a description still saying "Loading..." could end the wait early. I wrote a test for exactly that page, watched it fail, then fixed it.

6169 was merged on 6 November and shipped in career-ops v1.40.0 on 10 November. On the issue, the maintainer wrote: "Thanks for fixing it yourself."

What I check now, in any pipeline that sends fetched content to a model

  1. Count what the model received. Characters, not "page loaded". It is one log line.
  2. Don't mark work done because a reply came back. Mark it done when the input passed a check.
  3. Don't let the prompt promise tools the code doesn't send. The model will try to use them.
  4. Wait for content, not for a clock. A fixed sleep is a guess about someone else's server.

The tests passed the whole time, and the tracker looked full. That is what made it hard to see.

Links

  • Issue: https://github.com/career-ops-hq/career-ops/issues/5809
  • PRs: #5814, #5817, #6017, #6169
  • Release notes: https://github.com/career-ops-hq/career-ops/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

AI disclosure: I found and fixed these bugs with the help of AI coding tools (Claude Code), and drafted this post with Claude. Every number comes from the linked issue and pull requests, and I checked the text before publishing.

articles.title: I built an AI shopping agent that waits for the right price, and it can't overspend
articles.description: I have a habit. I find something I want, like a pair of headphones, decide it's a little too...
articles.body_html:
I have a habit. I find something I want, like a pair of headphones, decide it's a little too expensive, and then check the price every few days. I set alerts. I forget about them. When the sale finally happens, I miss it, or I see the email two days later and it's already over.

Price alerts only tell you. They don't act. So I built WaitForIt: you tell an AI agent what you want and the most you'll pay, and it watches the price and buys it for you when the price is right.

The tricky part wasn't the AI. It was trust. Would you let an AI spend your money while you're not looking? I wouldn't, unless there was a hard limit it couldn't cross. That limit became the core of the project.

How it works

  1. You type a wish in plain words: "Sony WH-CH720N headphones under $70".
