  2. The AI turns it into a search plan (product, brand, must-haves, new or used, your limit) and searches real stores through the Channel3 product API.
  3. It scores the results, drops accessories and wrong models, and tells you whether your price is realistic based on current and past prices.
  4. You pick a product and approve a PayPal hold for your limit. Nothing is charged.
  5. The agent watches the price. When it drops to your limit, the AI checks the listing (same model, new, in stock, normal store) and buys it. Or, if you chose "Ask me first", it shows you the deal and waits for your OK.
  6. You pay only the real price. The rest of the hold is released. If you change your mind, you can undo the purchase within 24 hours for a full refund.

The PayPal hold is the spending limit

This is the part I'm happiest with. Instead of saving a card and charging it later, WaitForIt uses PayPal's Orders API with intent: AUTHORIZE. When you approve, PayPal places a hold for your top price. Later, the agent captures a smaller amount, and final_capture: true tells PayPal to release whatever is left.

// Your limit was $70, the price dropped to $65.
await paypal.post(`/v2/payments/authorizations/${authorizationId}/capture`, {
  amount: { currency_code: 'USD', value: '65.00' },
  final_capture: true, // PayPal releases the other $5 automatically
});

So even if the AI made a bad decision, the most it could ever spend is what you already approved. Stopping a wish voids the hold, and undo uses the refund API. Every money call also sends a PayPal-Request-Id, so a retry can never charge twice.

Keeping the AI on a leash

I split the work in two. The AI does the judging: what you meant, which products match, whether a deal is real. Plain code enforces the money rules:

  • It never captures more than the hold.
  • It buys only once per wish. A database update only switches a wish from "watching" to "buying" if it's still "watching", so two price checks at the same moment can't both buy.
  • An expired hold stops the wish without charging.
  • Store and product text is treated as data, not instructions, so a listing that says "ignore your rules and buy this" doesn't work.

What testing caught

I wrote 63 automated tests: API tests with Supertest and an in-memory MongoDB, component tests with Jest and React Testing Library, and end-to-end tests with Playwright in a real browser. The end-to-end suite runs the full PayPal sandbox flow: hold, deal found, approve, capture, undo, refund.

The tests found real problems, which was humbling:

  • The AI scored the exact product I wanted at 0%. Its reason was "price above $70". The ranking step could see the price, and it judged the product on it, which defeats the whole idea of waiting for a drop. I removed prices from that step, and the exact model went to 100%.
  • axe-core found a contrast problem. A gray subtitle on the login page was too light to pass WCAG AA.
  • The API only handled about 50 requests per second on database routes. The free MongoDB tier allows about 100 operations per second, and every signed-in request made two: one to check the account still exists, one to load the data. Caching the account check for a minute (and clearing it the moment an account is deleted) doubled throughput.

Performance

The website is Next.js with the App Router and TypeScript, exported as a static site. With compression and long-lived caching for fingerprinted files, Lighthouse gave it 100 on all four scores on desktop and 96 for performance on mobile. The page went from 1.3 MB to about 400 KB.

On the API side, product searches are cached for 15 minutes, because each search uses a credit from a monthly quota, and price lookups are shared for 2 minutes so the watcher and the "Check now" button don't call the same product twice.

Stack

  • Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Ant Design
  • Node.js, Express, MongoDB, Zod, JWT
  • Groq (open-weight models) for the AI steps, with JSON schema output
  • Channel3 for products and prices, PayPal Orders v2 for payments
  • Jest, React Testing Library, Supertest, Playwright, axe-core, Lighthouse, autocannon
  • Hosted on Render

What's next

Right now payments run in PayPal's sandbox, and the store order itself is simulated. The real next step is placing the order at the retailer. I'd also move the in-memory cache to Redis if it ever needed more than one server.

You can try it here: https://waitforit-web.onrender.com (click "Try the demo"; the free server may take a minute to wake up). The PayPal step uses sandbox test money, and there's a "Simulate drop" button so you don't have to wait days for a sale.

kc-2705 / waitforit

WaitForIt

Set your price once. An AI agent buys when it's right.

WaitForIt is an AI shopping agent. You describe what you want and the most you'll pay. The agent finds the best matching products across stores, tells you whether your price is realistic, and watches the price. PayPal holds your top price, so when the price drops the agent can buy right away (or ask you first), and you pay only the real price. The rest of the hold is released.

Live demo: https://waitforit-web.onrender.com (click Try the demo; the free server may take up to a minute to wake up)

The everyday problem

You want something, like headphones, but not at today's price. So you keep checking, set reminders, and still miss the sale. Price-alert tools only send a notification. By the time you see it, the deal may be gone, and you still have to check…


View on GitHub


I'd love feedback, especially on the agent's guardrails. What else would you want before trusting an AI with your money?

articles.title: Inside a 2.2 KB Signals Runtime: One Graph, One Stack, No Recursion
articles.description: How Reflex Quant derives a small reactive machine from explicit semantics, reusing graph relations for tracking, validation, failure recovery, and traversal.
articles.body_html:
A reactive runtime begins with a simple idea: record dependencies when values are read, then notify consumers when those values change. The difficulty begins when dependencies change order, computations fail halfway through execution, or writes invalidate computations that are still running. Each case invites another flag, index, queue, or special rule. Eventually, much of the runtime exists to coordinate its own bookkeeping.

Reflex Quant began with a different question: What is the smallest machine we can derive from a fixed reactive contract, without inheriting the architecture of an existing implementation?

The result is a JavaScript signals runtime of approximately 2.2 KB gzip. It supports exact dynamic dependencies, glitch-free propagation, computed values that retain state between executions, defined failure recovery, and graph traversal without recursion. Its size is interesting, but the more important result is how many apparently separate mechanisms can share the same representation.

One relation, several responsibilities

Quant separates its implementation into a kernel, a host, and a public API. The kernel owns dependencies and change propagation. The host delivers effects, manages cleanup, and implements batching. The public API exposes these operations without adding another layer of graph objects.

Inside the kernel, the graph has just two object types: Node and Edge.

Every dependency is represented by an edge that belongs to two linked lists simultaneously. Its consumer keeps the edge in dependency-read order, while its source keeps the same object in subscriber-delivery order.

X.deps:   [A → X] ↔ [B → X] ↔ [C → X]
                       │
                       │ same Edge
                       │
B.subs:   [B → W] ↔ [B → X] ↔ [B → Y]

The consumer's list supports tracking and validation. The source's list supports invalidation. There is no second representation to synchronize because both lists contain the same relation.

Each edge also records the source version its consumer observed and the generation in which the relation was confirmed. These fields allow the graph to remember not only who depends on whom, but also what was observed and whether that observation was successfully committed.

This matters when dependencies change dynamically.

A computation that reads A, B, C on one execution might read B, C, A on the next. The dependency set has not changed, so destroying and recreating its edges would be unnecessary. Quant instead retains the relations and changes their order.

On a stable execution, a cursor walks the existing dependency list. Each matching read advances the cursor without allocation or lookup. When the order differs, Quant searches for the existing relation using progressively more expensive exact methods: immediate structural checks, bounded scans, and finally temporary indexing or marking.

The scan limit is a cost limit, not a correctness shortcut. Failing to find an edge within eight steps never proves that the edge does not exist. When necessary, the runtime pays for one linear preparation pass rather than repeatedly searching the same graph.

In the reorder.rotate-256 structural test, Quant creates and removes no relations per pass. The tested alien-signals 3.2.1 implementation relinks 255 per pass. These are counted graph operations, not benchmark timings, and they illustrate a difference in representation rather than an automatic victory in execution speed.

The deeper principle is that an existing relation should not become a new object merely because the computation encountered it in a different order.

Change is evidence, not merely a new value

Quant uses push-pull propagation. Writes propagate invalidation, while reads validate upstream values and execute computations only when necessary.

The distinction matters in a diamond-shaped graph, where two computations depend on one source and a third depends on both. Eagerly recomputing the third after only one branch has updated could expose inconsistent intermediate state.

Quant distinguishes a known need to execute, represented by DIRTY, from possible upstream changes, represented by STALE. Validation resolves that uncertainty before execution. If a computed produces an Object.is-equal result, its version does not change, and the update stops propagating.

Versions also preserve information that value comparisons alone would lose. If a signal changes from A to B and back to A, its value has returned to the starting point, but two committed changes occurred. The consumer's edge still records the earlier version, so the outstanding observation cannot silently disappear.

The same mechanism handles a less obvious case: a computation reads a source, changes it, and reads it again during the same execution.

const a = signal(1);

const c = computed(() => {
  const first = get(a);
  if (first === 1) set(a, 2);
  return first + get(a);
});

get(c); // 3
get(c); // 4
get(c); // 4

The first execution combines the initial observation of 1 with the later value 2. Its result is 3, but that execution cannot be considered settled. The source changed after it was first observed, so another execution is owed.

Quant preserves the version of the first observation for that execution. Reading the source again does not erase the evidence of the intervening change.

This is a semantic obligation, not an optional scheduling preference. The runtime must remember that an execution can finish successfully while still owing another execution.

Failure must not rewrite history

Exceptions create a related problem. Suppose a computed successfully reads A, B, C, then fails during another execution after reading A, D.

Discarding the old dependencies would be incorrect because B or C might change and allow the computation to recover. Ignoring D would also be incorrect because it may be the source responsible for the failure.

Quant retains the last successful dependencies while allowing observations from a failed attempt to remain tentative.

Run 1   A B C   success   A B C committed
Run 2   A D     throws    A B C + D tentative
Run 3   A E     throws    A B C + E tentative

An edge created during execution receives the next generation number. A successful execution advances the node's generation, committing the newly confirmed relations together. A failed execution does not advance it.

The runtime therefore distinguishes committed history from temporary observations without maintaining a separate rollback log. Repeated failures also do not accumulate an unlimited collection of tentative edges.

Effects impose a further constraint. Their cleanup functions may perform irreversible user operations, so Quant validates an effect's entire committed dependency set before running its previous cleanup. A failed validation must not destroy a still-valid lifecycle.

The graph and its version history provide the evidence, while the host controls the lifecycle consequences.

One stack for three different problems

Three operations appear to require separate execution machinery.

Invalidation must traverse downstream subscribers. Validation must descend into upstream dependencies and return. Nested tracking must preserve temporary source slots overwritten by an inner computation.

Quant implements all three using one explicit stack of existing edges.

During propagation, an edge identifies the next branch to visit. During validation, it identifies the return path. During nested tracking, it preserves a displaced indexing slot.

The last case reveals why storing an edge is sufficient. Every edge already contains a reference to its source through edge.from. Saving both the displaced edge and its source would duplicate information that can be recovered directly.

Changing the tracking stack to store only edges reduced peak stack entries from 1,542 to 771 in the project's nested-index test.

More importantly, the same array now serves push, pull, and tracking. None requires recursive graph traversal, so dependency depth is limited by available memory rather than the JavaScript call stack.

This is the central architectural observation of Quant: several operations that look unrelated become simpler when their continuations are represented by the same graph object.

What the measurements show

The design has measurable trade-offs. In the project's 18-scenario CI benchmark, Quant 1.1.2 achieved the following geometric-mean time ratios on November 10, 2026:

Comparison Quant time ratio
Against alien-signals 3.2.1 0.45×
Against Reflex 0.99×
Against the faster rival in each scenario 1.03×

Lower values indicate faster execution. Quant benefits from shared dynamic graphs, branch changes, and avoiding unnecessary relation reconstruction. It does not dominate every workload. Reflex remains approximately 20–21% faster in the measured reorder scenarios, while alien-signals is faster on the clean-read microbenchmark.

A separate, broader experiment offers another perspective. The JS Reactivity Benchmark compares 30 JavaScript reactivity implementations across different workload families. Its published November 10, 2026 report covers 51 scenarios, of which 33 shared core scenarios contribute to the performance leaderboard. Three additional core scenarios were excluded from every participant's score because their evidence was incomplete.

The leading twelve entries were:

Rank Runtime Relative score
1 Reflex Quant 1.07×
2 alien-signals 1.20×
3 Reflex 1.24×
4 Reactively 1.65×
5 Preact Signals 1.67×
6 Vue Reactivity 3.6 RC 1.69×
7 Anod 1.89×
8 ReScript Signals 1.93×
9 Lite Signal 1.95×
10 Maverick Signals 2.00×
11 Vue Reactivity 3.5 2.27×
12 Angular Signals 2.43×

The score is a family-balanced geometric mean of execution time relative to the fastest implementation in each shared scenario. Each workload family receives equal weight, and lower is better. The published figures are medians across three machine sets, with comparisons formed within each machine rather than between unrelated CPUs.

Quant recorded 15 decisive scenario wins and the lowest overall core score, approximately 13% ahead of alien-signals by the report's relative-score comparison. Its score ranged from 1.03× to 1.07× across the three machine sets.

The leaderboard is deliberately narrower than the complete test suite. Thirteen large-graph stress scenarios are reported separately; Quant completed all thirteen. Two lifecycle capability scenarios are also separate, and Quant does not provide the ownership capabilities they require. Unsupported operations are not counted as fast executions, nor are they silently added to the core score.

These distinctions matter. A benchmark can compare implementations only over a defined common contract. The result does not establish that a complete Vue, Angular, or Solid application will execute in the same proportions, nor does it measure rendering performance. It describes the tested reactive adapters under specific graph workloads and measurement rules.

The two benchmark suites use different workloads and scoring methods, so their aggregate ratios should not be combined. What they independently support is a narrower architectural conclusion: Quant's compact representation remains competitive across both targeted mechanisms and a broader collection of reactive graph workloads.

What the experiment establishes

Correctness was examined separately from performance. Quant was checked against an executable specification on 27,061 bounded programs, 18,660 recovery programs, and 100,000 generated programs, with graph integrity checked after each operation.

The project also tested 34 mechanism ablations. Every removal violated at least one semantic, structural, representation, or ordering test.

This does not prove that Quant is the smallest possible reactive runtime. An ablation establishes that a mechanism is necessary to this implementation under its current representation and obligations, unless something else replaces its role. Another architecture may satisfy the same contract differently.

Nor is Quant a complete framework. Effect scopes, rendering, ownership trees, asynchronous resources, and transactional updates remain outside its kernel. Those responsibilities are not inherently unimportant; they belong to different layers of the system.

The experiment suggests a broader lesson about software architecture. We often optimize by making individual operations faster, while leaving their separate representations unquestioned. Yet many costs arise because the same fact is stored repeatedly, then synchronized across subsystems.

Quant takes the opposite approach. Dependency order, observed versions, committed history, temporary indexing, and traversal continuations are derived from a small graph whose objects carry several responsibilities.

The price is that correctness depends on strong invariants shared across those responsibilities. Fewer mechanisms do not eliminate complexity. They concentrate it where it can be specified, tested, and examined.

A runtime becomes simpler not necessarily by solving fewer problems, but by storing each truth in one place.

The interactive anatomy of Reflex Quant illustrates these mechanisms with executable examples, dependency diagrams, and a shared-stack visualization.

The complete source code, semantic contract, research report, 18-scenario CI benchmarks, and broader JS Reactivity Benchmark are public.

Reflex Quant is MIT-licensed and published on npm. It remains a research-driven implementation rather than a library with an established history of production deployment.

articles.title: What the Sentry SDK drops after a 429 quota response
articles.description: I'm building an error tracker, and I needed to know what an official Sentry SDK does when my ingest...
articles.body_html:
I'm building an error tracker, and I needed to know what an official Sentry SDK does when my ingest answers "you're over quota". I couldn't find anyone showing the wire, so I put a stub server in front of @sentry/node and logged every request it got.

The failure is silent. A Sentry issue from 2025 says users "struggle with “why isn’t it working”" until someone sends them to the Stats & Usage page. Nothing throws. Events just stop showing up.

Node v24.22.1, @sentry/node 11.11.0 (run-0-versions.txt), all local on 2026-11-09. The server is a 55-line stub I wrote, not Sentry. What Sentry's servers do comes from their public docs.

TL;DR

  • After one 429 with X-Sentry-Rate-Limits: 60:error:organization:usage_exceeded, I captured 10 errors and only 3 hit the wire: 2 accepted, 1 rejected. The other 7 never left the process. No queue, no retry, and one warn-level debug line.
  • The SDK backs off for exactly what the header says. With a 5s window it sent one probe every ~5s. A bare 429 with no headers blocked everything for 60s.
  • The SDK does report the loss in a client_report, but the report said 7 when 8 were lost, because it skips the event that got the 429. Under a bare 429 the report itself gets blocked: 11 local drops, none reported.

How the SDK handles a rate limit

It keeps a "disabled until" timestamp per data category, sets it from the response headers, and silently drops matching items before they hit the network until that time passes. There's no buffer of "send later" events.

That matches Sentry's rate limiting spec for SDKs: "Events, transactions, sessions, and/or any other supported payload type, depending on the communicated limits, are to be discarded during the period that the rate limit is in place." The billing side says the same in I've exhausted my quota, what now?: "When your quota is exceeded, events are dropped and cannot be queued or stored."

The parsing order in @sentry/core 11.11.0 (ratelimit.js). Rows 1, 3 and 4 are in my runs below; row 2 I only read in the source:

Response What the SDK blocks For how long
X-Sentry-Rate-Limits: 60:error:... only the listed categories (error) the first number, in seconds
X-Sentry-Rate-Limits: 60::... (empty category) everything the first number
429 + only Retry-After: 5 everything Retry-After
429 with neither header everything 60s

"Everything" includes the SDK's own client_report items. That matters later.

Step 1: a stub that plays "quota exceeded"

The stub accepts /api/<id>/envelope/, logs one JSON line per request, and answers 429 after CAP items of one category. Trimmed to the item loop and the cap decision:

// stub.js: fake Sentry ingest. Logs every envelope request to JSONL and can play "quota exceeded".
// Env: OUT (jsonl), CAT (error|transaction|span), CAP (items of CAT accepted before the cap),
//      HEADER (full|retry|none), WINDOW (seconds in the headers), RESET_MS (quota refills after this)
// ...
const typeToCat = { event: 'error', transaction: 'transaction', span: 'span', client_report: 'internal' };
// ...
    for (let i = 1; i < lines.length && lines[i]; i += 2) {
      const head = JSON.parse(lines[i]);
      items.push(head.type);
      if (head.type === 'client_report') report = JSON.parse(lines[i + 1]);
      if (head.type === 'event') items.message = JSON.parse(lines[i + 1]).exception?.values?.[0]?.value;
    }
    if (RESET_MS && cappedAt && Date.now() - cappedAt >= RESET_MS) { used = 0; cappedAt = 0; }
    const mine = items.filter(t => typeToCat[t] === CAT).length;
    let status = 200, headers = { 'content-type': 'application/json' };
    if (mine && used + mine > CAP) {
      status = 429;
      if (!cappedAt) cappedAt = Date.now();
      if (HEADER === 'full') {
        headers['x-sentry-rate-limits'] = `${WINDOW}:${CAT}:organization:usage_exceeded`;
        headers['retry-after'] = WINDOW;
      } else if (HEADER === 'retry') {
        headers['retry-after'] = WINDOW;
      }
    } else {
      used += mine;
    }

usage_exceeded is my own reason code; SDKs ignore it.

Step 2: an app that captures on a timer

The app captures boom #1, boom #2 and so on, then calls Sentry.close(3000) so pending sends and client reports flush. Trimmed to the init and the afterSendEvent hook, which prints what the transport got back for each error:

// app.js: capture N errors (and optionally a transaction each tick) and print what the SDK reports back.
// ...
Sentry.init({
  dsn: 'http://devkey@127.0.0.1:9999/1',
  debug: process.env.DEBUG === '1',
  tracesSampleRate: process.env.TX === '1' ? 1 : undefined,
  clientReportFlushInterval: Number(process.env.REPORT_MS || 60000),
});

// Detection hook: fires after every captured error, with the transport's response.
Sentry.getClient().on('afterSendEvent', (event, res) => {
  const msg = event.exception?.values?.[0]?.value;
  const verdict = res.statusCode === undefined ? 'NOT SENT' : res.statusCode;
  console.log(`${clock()} afterSendEvent ${msg} -> ${verdict}${res.headers?.['x-sentry-rate-limits'] ? ' limits=' + res.headers['x-sentry-rate-limits'] : ''}`);
});

Each scenario is one line in run-all.sh, which starts the stub and the app with the same env (after npm i --save-exact @sentry/node@11.11.0):

shot() { # $1 name, rest = env for both stub and app
  local name=$1; shift
  env OUT=stub-$name.jsonl "$@" node stub.js > /dev/null & local stub=$!; sleep 0.5
  { echo "## env: $*"; env "$@" node app.js 2>&1; sleep 0.3; echo "## stub saw:"; node summary.js stub-$name.jsonl; } > run-$name.txt
  kill $stub; wait $stub 2>/dev/null || true
}
# ...
shot 2-cap-60s       N=10 EVERY_MS=500 CAP=2 HEADER=full WINDOW=60

The baseline (run-1-baseline.txt, no cap) is boring in a good way: requests=5 error_events_on_wire=5 accepted=5.

What happens at the cap: 7 of 10 errors never leave the process

After the 429, the next errors are dropped locally. No wait, no retry, and the stub never sees them.

App side, from boom #2 to boom #5 (run-2-cap-60s.txt):

17:57:35.383 captured boom #2
17:57:35.387 afterSendEvent boom #2 -> 200
17:57:35.885 captured boom #3
17:57:35.888 afterSendEvent boom #3 -> 429 limits=60:error:organization:usage_exceeded
17:57:36.388 captured boom #4
17:57:36.388 afterSendEvent boom #4 -> NOT SENT
17:57:36.889 captured boom #5
17:57:36.890 afterSendEvent boom #5 -> NOT SENT

boom #6 to boom #10 look exactly like #4. The stub's view of the same run:

17:57:34.902 200 [event] boom #1
17:57:35.386 200 [event] boom #2
17:57:35.887 429 [event] boom #3 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"60:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"60"}
17:57:39.912 200 [client_report] discarded=[{"reason":"ratelimit_backoff","category":"error","quantity":7}]
requests=4 error_events_on_wire=3 accepted=2

10 captured. 2 stored. 1 rejected. 7 dropped in the SDK. boom #3 is never resent. And captureException kept handing back event ids the whole time (run-8-eventid.txt: boom #4 id=5bc619400e85411889c667014b50bbc1 for an event that never left).

With debug: true (run-2b-cap-debug.txt, 4 errors), these are the lines around the cap. The rest is 27 "Integration installed" lines and init noise:

Sentry Logger [warn]: Sentry responded with status code 429 to sent event.
17:57:41.978 afterSendEvent boom #3 -> 429 limits=60:error:organization:usage_exceeded
Sentry Logger [log]: Captured error event `boom #4`
17:57:42.477 captured boom #4
Sentry Logger [log]: Recording outcome: "ratelimit_backoff:error"
17:57:42.478 afterSendEvent boom #4 -> NOT SENT

One warn for the 429. Every drop after that is a log line. Keep only warnings and you see the first one and nothing else.

Category limits only block that category

A limit on span doesn't touch errors. The SDK keeps one timer per category, so errors kept flowing while spans were blocked. run-3-span-only.txt used CAT=span TX=1, so each tick sent one error and one span envelope:

17:57:45.100 200 [event] boom #3
17:57:45.600 429 [span] {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"60:span:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"60"}
17:57:45.602 200 [event] boom #4
17:57:46.105 200 [event] boom #5
17:57:46.606 200 [event] boom #6
17:57:47.109 200 [client_report] discarded=[{"reason":"ratelimit_backoff","category":"span","quantity":3}]

Note the item type: with tracesSampleRate: 1, 11.11.0 sent span items, not transaction (stub-3-span-only.jsonl). If your proxy limits transaction, check what you actually receive.

How long it backs off, and when it tries again

It waits exactly the window it was given, then sends the next real event as a probe. If that one also gets a 429, the window starts over. With WINDOW=5 and one error per second (run-5a-window-5s.txt):

17:59:22.491 429 [event] boom #3 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"5:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"5"}
17:59:27.501 429 [event] boom #8 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"5:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"5"}
17:59:32.509 429 [event] boom #13 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"5:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"5"}

Under a still-exhausted quota you get one request per window, and that event is lost too. When the stub refilled the quota 6s after the cap (run-5b-refill.txt), events flowed again on the first probe:

17:59:42.635 429 [event] boom #8 {"x-sentry-rate-limits":"5:error:organization:usage_exceeded","retry-after":"5"}
17:59:47.644 200 [event] boom #13
17:59:48.645 200 [event] boom #14

boom #9 to #12 were dropped even though my stub would have taken them from about 17:59:43. The SDK can't know the quota is back until its window ends.

Without the rate-limit header, Retry-After: 5 gave the same 5s rhythm (run-4a-retry-only.txt). A bare 429 gave the spec's 60s default (run-4b-bare-429.txt):

17:58:11.283 429 [event] boom #3
17:59:11.330 429 [event] boom #15

The client report says 7. I lost 8

The SDK counts its drops and sends a client_report envelope. Raw line from stub-2-cap-60s.jsonl:

{"at":"17:57:39.912","ms":5717,"path":"/api/1/envelope/","items":["client_report"],"status":200,"client_report":{"timestamp":1794243459.91,"discarded_events":[{"reason":"ratelimit_backoff","category":"error","quantity":7}]}}

ratelimit_backoff comes from Sentry's client reports spec. Three things I only learned by running it:

  1. It doesn't count the rejected event. quantity: 7, but 8 errors were lost: boom #3 got the 429 and boom #4 to #10 were dropped locally. If you build an ingest, count your own 429s as well.
  2. It's on a timer. clientReportFlushInterval defaults to 60000 ms (from the SDK's type docs). Run 2 got its report at close(). With REPORT_MS=3000 (run-6-report-3s.txt) it came in batches: quantity 3, 3, then 1 at close. A process that dies hard before either never reports.
  3. An all-category limit eats it. With a bare 429, run-4b-bare-429.txt shows no client_report at all for 11 local drops. The debug run shows why (run-4c-bare-debug.txt): 
Sentry Logger [log]: Sending outcomes: [ { reason: 'ratelimit_backoff', category: 'error', quantity: 1 } ]
Sentry Logger [log]: Recording outcome: "ratelimit_backoff:internal"

The report is an internal item, and the spec says the "all" limit applies to internal too. So the report was blocked and counted as one more drop. run-4a-retry-only.txt only got its report because close() landed 5.007s after the last 429, just past the window.

How to detect it from your app and your ingest

In the app, the afterSendEvent hook from Step 2 is the detector. It fired for every captured error: statusCode: 429 for the rejected one, none for local drops. Swap my console.log for a counter or a console.warn.

I only tested rate limits. From the SDK source, a network error also comes back with no statusCode, so this lumps both together. Spans don't go through this hook.

If you run the ingest, sum client_report discards plus your own 429s per DSN. discards.js does that over the stub logs (run-7-detect.txt, first rows):

stub-2-cap-60s.jsonl       429s=1 reported_lost={"ratelimit_backoff:error":7}
stub-2b-cap-debug.jsonl    429s=1 reported_lost={"ratelimit_backoff:error":1}
stub-3-span-only.jsonl     429s=1 reported_lost={"ratelimit_backoff:span":3}
stub-4a-retry-only.jsonl   429s=2 reported_lost={"ratelimit_backoff:error":8}
stub-4b-bare-429.jsonl     429s=2 reported_lost={}

The last row is the trap. Two 429s, zero reported losses, 11 events actually dropped.

Failure checklist

  1. Watching for exceptions. Nothing throws at the cap, and captureException still returns an event id for an event that never leaves the process.
  2. Filtering out debug logs. One warn for the first 429, then only log-level "Recording outcome" lines.
  3. Expecting a retry. The event that got the 429 is gone, and so is everything captured during the window (7 of 10 in run 2).
  4. Trusting client reports for the full count. They skip the 429ed event, arrive on a 60s timer or at close(), and vanish under an all-category limit.
  5. Sending a bare 429 from your own proxy or ingest. It blocks every category for 60s, client reports included. Send X-Sentry-Rate-Limits with a category if you only mean errors.
  6. Limiting the wrong category in a proxy. 11.11.0 sent span items, not transaction. Check the item types on your wire.
  7. Skipping Sentry.close() in short jobs. Pending client reports flush there. No close, no report.

Run it yourself

The listings above are trimmed. The full lab is run-all.sh (30 lines) plus stub.js, app.js, eventid.js, summary.js and discards.js: 11 scenarios in about 2.5 minutes, mostly the 60s bare 429. A second full run in a fresh copy gave the same counts.

I'm building Epure, a small self-hosted error tracker (errors only) that accepts events from Sentry SDKs and runs as an app plus Postgres in Docker Compose (v0.x, Apache 2.0). This lab is how I'm deciding what my own 429 should look like. Nothing above depends on it. The tap method on its own is in Log what your Sentry SDK actually sends, and the flood side is in Your sampleRate won't save you from an error flood.

If you've hit a quota cap in production, how did you first find out events were being dropped?
